title: Neonatal Resp Distress
subtitle: Tachypnea, grunting, retractions, cyanosis, O₂ need

root.label: Neonatal Resp Distress
root.description: Tachypnea, grunting, retractions, cyanosis, O₂ need

content.html:
Respiratory distress is the most common reason for NICU admission. It can result from pulmonary disease, cardiac disease, or systemic illness (sepsis, metabolic). A systematic approach differentiates the etiology.

Signs of respiratory distress:

  • Tachypnea (RR >60/min sustained)
  • Grunting (expiratory — maintaining positive end-expiratory pressure to prevent alveolar collapse)
  • Nasal flaring
  • Retractions (subcostal, intercostal, suprasternal)
  • Cyanosis (central)
  • Apnea / periodic breathing
  • Oxygen requirement (SpO₂ <90% in room air)

Silverman-Andersen Respiratory Severity Score (0–10):

Score 0–3: mild; 4–6: moderate; 7–10: severe (likely needs ventilatory support)

ℹ️ Preterm SpO₂ targets: 90–95%. Avoid sustained SpO₂ >95% in preterm infants — hyperoxia increases ROP, BPD, and mortality (BOOST-II, COT, SUPPORT trials). Lower alarm at 89%, upper alarm at 95%.

Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS): Caused by surfactant deficiency in preterm infants. Incidence inversely proportional to gestational age — ~80% at 28 wk, ~50% at 32 wk, ~15% at 34 wk.

  • CXR: bilateral ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms, reduced lung volumes
  • Progressive respiratory failure over first 12–48 hours
  • Improves after 48–72 hours as endogenous surfactant production increases

Surfactant Administration — 2022 European Consensus (Sweet et al.):

  • Indications: FiO₂ >0.30 on CPAP in infants <30 wk, or FiO₂ >0.40 on CPAP at any GA with RDS
  • Agent: Poractant alfa (Curosurf) 200 mg/kg preferred first dose (superior to 100 mg/kg dose per Ramanathan et al.); beractant (Survanta) 100 mg/kg; calfactant (Infasurf) 105 mg/kg
  • Repeat dosing: May give up to 2–3 additional doses if ongoing O₂ requirement >0.30–0.40 on CPAP
  • Route: LISA (Less Invasive Surfactant Administration) or INSURE (INtubate-SURfactant-Extubate) preferred over prolonged intubation

CPAP-First Approach:

  • SUPPORT trial (NEJM 2010): Early CPAP non-inferior to intubation/surfactant for death/BPD in ELBW
  • Start CPAP 5–7 cmH₂O in delivery room for spontaneously breathing preterm infants
  • LISA (thin catheter surfactant on CPAP) reduces need for MV vs INSURE
  • Avoid routine intubation — keep on CPAP unless FiO₂ escalating or apnea/respiratory failure
✓ Less-Invasive Surfactant Administration (LISA): Surfactant given via thin catheter while infant remains on CPAP, avoiding intubation. Multiple RCTs show reduced BPD, less MV, shorter NICU stay vs standard intubation.

PaCO₂ (permissive)45–65 mmHgPermissive hypercapnia reduces ventilator-induced lung injury (accept pH >7.20)
Tidal volume4–6 mL/kgVolume-targeted ventilation reduces BPD vs pressure-targeted
PEEP5–8 cmH₂OMaintain FRC; prevent atelectrauma
PIPLowest achieving adequate TVMinimize barotrauma

AgentDoseVolumeNotes
Poractant alfa (Curosurf)200 mg/kg initial2.5 mL/kgHigher dose superior; repeat 100 mg/kg q12h PRN
Beractant (Survanta)100 mg/kg4 mL/kgRepeat q6h PRN up to 4 doses
Calfactant (Infasurf)105 mg/kg3 mL/kgRepeat q12h PRN up to 3 doses

LISA (Less Invasive Surfactant Administration):

  1. Infant on CPAP (spontaneously breathing)
  2. Direct laryngoscopy to visualize vocal cords
  3. Insert thin catheter (16F feeding tube or dedicated LISA catheter) through cords into trachea
  4. Instill surfactant slowly over 1–3 minutes while infant continues to breathe on CPAP
  5. Remove catheter. Continue CPAP.
  6. Avoid positive pressure ventilation during/after procedure
✓ LISA reduces need for mechanical ventilation by ~30% and may reduce BPD compared to INSURE or standard intubation methods.

BPD Prevention Bundle:

  • Antenatal steroids (most effective single intervention)
  • CPAP-first approach (avoid intubation if possible)
  • LISA/INSURE for surfactant delivery
  • Volume-targeted ventilation (Tv 4–6 mL/kg) when MV needed
  • Permissive hypercapnia (PaCO₂ 45–65, pH >7.20)
  • SpO₂ targets 90–95% (avoid hyperoxia)
  • Caffeine citrate starting from birth
  • Minimize postnatal steroids (consider low-dose hydrocortisone per PREMILOC)
  • Breast milk nutrition (reduces inflammation)
  • Vitamin A supplementation (modest benefit; underutilized)

Caffeine Citrate (CAP Trial, Schmidt et al., NEJM 2006):

  • Loading: 20 mg/kg IV/PO
  • Maintenance: 5–10 mg/kg/day IV/PO once daily
  • Start as early as possible (within first 48h of life) in infants <1250g
  • Benefits: 36% reduction in BPD, improved neurodevelopment at 18–21 months and 5 years, earlier extubation, reduced PDA treatment
  • One of the MOST evidence-based therapies in neonatology

Non-Invasive Ventilation Escalation:

ModeSettingsWhen
CPAP5–8 cmH₂OFirst-line for RDS
HFNC (High-Flow)2–8 L/minStep-down from CPAP; similar efficacy in mild RDS
NIPPV/BiPAPPIP 14–20, PEEP 5–7, Rate 20–40Rescue from CPAP failure; may reduce intubation
NHFOVMAP 8–12, Hz 8–12, ΔP 25–35Emerging; limited evidence but growing use

Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN): Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. Most common cause of respiratory distress in term/late-preterm infants.

  • Risk factors: C-section (no labor = no catecholamine surge for fluid clearance), late-preterm, maternal DM, precipitous delivery, male sex
  • Self-limited: resolves in 24–72 hours
  • CXR: hyperinflation, perihilar streaking, fluid in fissures, mild cardiomegaly

TTN is a diagnosis of exclusion. Must rule out:

  • Pneumonia/sepsis (clinical overlap — consider empiric antibiotics if risk factors present)
  • Pneumothorax (asymmetric CXR, acute deterioration)
  • Congenital heart disease (persistent hypoxemia, murmur)
  • RDS in late-preterm (can coexist with TTN)
⚠️ If FiO₂ >0.40 or symptoms persist >72 hours, reconsider the diagnosis. True TTN rarely requires more than low-flow O₂ and resolves within 72h.

• Supportive care: supplemental O₂ to maintain SpO₂ >90–95%
  • CPAP may help if moderate distress (5–6 cmH₂O)
  • NPO until RR <60–80 (aspiration risk with tachypnea); IV fluids
  • No benefit from furosemide or racemic epinephrine
  • Monitor for improvement — expect resolution by 24–72h

Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS): Chemical pneumonitis and mechanical obstruction from aspirated meconium, causing ball-valve effect (air trapping), surfactant inactivation, and intense inflammatory response.

  • Occurs in ~5% of deliveries with meconium-stained amniotic fluid
  • Risk factors: post-term (>42 wk), fetal distress/asphyxia, thick meconium
  • CXR: patchy, coarse, irregular opacities; hyperinflation; may see pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum
  • NRP 2020: Routine tracheal suctioning of vigorous meconium-stained infants is NOT recommended. Intubation and suctioning only if infant is NOT breathing or HR <100 after initial steps.

1. Respiratory support: Supplemental O₂ → CPAP → mechanical ventilation if failing
  2. Surfactant: Consider if intubated and FiO₂ >0.50; may improve oxygenation by overcoming surfactant inactivation. Bolus lavage technique studied but not standard.
  3. Avoid overventilation: Air trapping → pneumothorax risk. Use longer expiratory times, avoid high PEEP.
  4. Antibiotics: Empiric amp/gent (meconium is a bacterial growth medium; risk of secondary infection)
  5. Supportive: Temperature control, fluid management, treat acidosis, minimal stimulation
  6. ECMO: Consider if severe hypoxemia despite maximal therapy (OI >40 sustained)

Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension (PPHN) complicates ~30% of MAS.

  • Mechanism: meconium causes pulmonary vasoconstriction + inflammation → right-to-left shunting through PDA/foramen ovale
  • Diagnosis: pre-/post-ductal SpO₂ difference >5–10%; echo shows elevated PA pressures, R→L shunting
  • Treatment: See PPHN branch

Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN): Failure of normal postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance → right-to-left shunting through PDA and/or foramen ovale → severe hypoxemia.

Etiologies:

  • Maladaptation: MAS, pneumonia, RDS, TTN (normal lung vasculature, abnormal transition)
  • Maldevelopment: CDH, pulmonary hypoplasia (abnormal vascular structure)
  • Idiopathic: Remodeled muscular pulmonary arteries (associated with maternal SSRI use, NSAID exposure)

Diagnostic evaluation:

  1. Pre-/post-ductal SpO₂: Right hand (pre-ductal) vs either foot (post-ductal). Difference >5–10% suggests R→L ductal shunting.
  2. Echocardiogram: Elevated RV pressure, TR jet velocity (estimates PA pressure), direction of shunting across PDA and PFO, rule out structural heart disease.
  3. CXR: May show underlying lung disease or clear lungs (idiopathic PPHN); may have decreased pulmonary vascularity.
  4. Blood gas: Severe hypoxemia (PaO₂ often <50 mmHg despite 100% FiO₂)
  5. Oxygenation Index (OI): OI = (MAP × FiO₂ × 100) / PaO₂. OI >25 = severe; OI >40 = consider ECMO.

Stepwise Treatment:

  1. Optimize ventilation: Gentle ventilation targeting SpO₂ 90–97%. Correct acidosis. Maintain normal PaCO₂ (35–45 mmHg; mild alkalosis may help acutely but avoid sustained hyperventilation).
  2. Sedation: Minimize stimulation and agitation (worsen PVR). Fentanyl or morphine infusion.
  3. Inotropes: Maintain systemic BP > PA pressure. Dopamine, milrinone (PDE3 inhibitor — reduces PVR AND improves cardiac output), epinephrine.
  4. Inhaled Nitric Oxide (iNO): Start at 20 ppm if OI >15–25. Selective pulmonary vasodilator. ~60% response rate.
  5. Surfactant: If underlying parenchymal disease (MAS, pneumonia, RDS).
  6. High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation (HFOV): If conventional ventilation failing (optimizes lung recruitment + reduces barotrauma).
  7. ECMO: If OI >40 sustained, or OI >60 on any single measurement, despite maximal medical therapy. VA-ECMO preferred. Survival ~75–90% for respiratory ECMO.

iNO Protocol:

ParameterProtocol
Starting dose20 ppm
Assess responseImprovement in PaO₂ or SpO₂ within 30–60 min
Non-responderNo significant improvement at 20 ppm after 30–60 min → unlikely to respond to higher doses
WeaningOnce FiO₂ <0.60 and stable: wean iNO to 10 → 5 → 2 → 1 ppm → off. DO NOT abruptly discontinue (causes rebound PH).
MonitoringMethemoglobin levels q12–24h (keep <5%); NO₂ levels
🚨 NEVER abruptly stop iNO. Rebound pulmonary hypertension can be life-threatening. Always wean gradually over hours to days.

• Start at 20 ppm if OI >15–25 or persistent hypoxemia despite optimal ventilation
  • Assess response within 30–60 minutes (↑ PaO₂ by ≥20 mmHg)
  • No benefit from doses >20 ppm (increases methemoglobin and NO₂ toxicity)
  • Non-responders: consider sildenafil, milrinone, HFOV, ECMO

1. Once FiO₂ weaned to <0.60 and hemodynamically stable
  2. Wean iNO: 20 → 10 → 5 → 2 → 1 ppm (each step over hours)
  3. At 1 ppm, trial off with careful monitoring
  4. If desaturation on wean: increase back to last effective dose and retry later
  5. Rebound PPHN may occur — have iNO ready to restart

ECMO Indications in PPHN:

  • OI >40 sustained (3–5 measurements) despite maximal therapy
  • OI >60 on any single measurement
  • Acute decompensation with cardiovascular collapse
  • PaO₂ <40 mmHg despite 100% FiO₂ and iNO at 20 ppm
  • GA ≥34 weeks and weight ≥2 kg (relative requirements)
  • Survival: 75–90% for respiratory ECMO

Relative contraindications:

  • GA <34 weeks or weight <2 kg (high IVH risk from anticoagulation)
  • Severe IVH (Grade III–IV)
  • Major congenital anomalies incompatible with meaningful survival
  • Irreversible lung disease (severe pulmonary hypoplasia with inadequate lung tissue)
  • Mechanical ventilation >14 days (lower survival; increased lung injury)

Neonatal pneumothorax: 1–2% of all neonates (many asymptomatic). Higher in preterm on MV (4–15%) and MAS (10–20%).

  • Tension pneumothorax: Mediastinal shift, cardiovascular compromise, EMERGENT needle decompression
  • Transillumination: Fiberoptic light on chest wall — affected side glows brighter. Quick bedside test.
  • CXR: Hyperlucent hemithorax, visible visceral pleural line, mediastinal shift (tension), collapsed lung

Needle Decompression (for tension pneumothorax — do NOT wait for CXR):

  1. Identify affected side (decreased breath sounds, shift of heart sounds, transillumination positive)
  2. 18–22 gauge angiocatheter attached to 20 mL syringe via 3-way stopcock
  3. Insert at 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (or 4th ICS, anterior axillary line)
  4. Direct needle over the TOP of the rib (avoid neurovascular bundle on inferior rib margin)
  5. Aspirate air → rush of air confirms pneumothorax → stabilization of vitals
  6. Leave catheter in place as temporary drain until chest tube placed

Chest Tube Placement:

  • Indicated for: symptomatic pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax (after needle decompression), ongoing air leak
  • Site: 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
  • Size: 8–10 Fr for term; 8 Fr for preterm
  • Connect to underwater seal with -10 to -20 cmH₂O suction
  • Confirm position on CXR
  • Remove when no air leak for 24–48 hours and lung re-expanded
🚨 Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. If acute deterioration + unilateral decreased breath sounds + hemodynamic compromise → NEEDLE DECOMPRESSION IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait for CXR.

node.label: Apnea of Prematurity
node.description: Caffeine first-line · Rule out secondary causes

content.html:
Apnea of prematurity (AOP): Cessation of breathing for ≥20 seconds, OR shorter pause accompanied by bradycardia (<100 bpm) and/or oxygen desaturation (SpO₂ <80%). Three types: central (no effort), obstructive (effort against obstruction), mixed (most common, ~50%).

  • Affects virtually all infants <28 weeks; ~50% of infants 30–34 weeks
  • AOP is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION — always rule out secondary causes first

Always rule out secondary causes before attributing to AOP:

CategoryCauses
InfectionSepsis, NEC, meningitis — apnea may be first sign of LOS
NeurologicIVH, seizures, hydrocephalus
MetabolicHypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hyponatremia, IEM
ThermalHypothermia or hyperthermia
RespiratoryAirway obstruction, RDS worsening, pneumothorax
GIGER (controversial association), NEC
HematologicAnemia (Hb <7–8 g/dL)
DrugsMaternal opioids, magnesium, sedatives
⚠️ New onset or worsening apnea in a previously stable preterm infant = SEPSIS until proven otherwise. Full sepsis evaluation before attributing to AOP.

Treatment:

  • Caffeine citrate — first-line. Loading: 20 mg/kg PO/IV. Maintenance: 5–10 mg/kg/day. Most important pharmacologic intervention.
  • CPAP (5–7 cmH₂O) — prevents obstructive component by splinting airway and maintaining FRC
  • HFNC (1–4 L/min) — alternative to CPAP for mild cases
  • NIPPV — may be more effective than CPAP alone for refractory apnea
  • Doxapram — second-line respiratory stimulant; limited use in US
  • Transfusion — if anemia contributing (Hb <8 g/dL with symptomatic apnea)
  • Positioning — prone positioning reduces apnea frequency in NICU (but NOT for home sleep — always supine for SIDS prevention)

content.html:
CDH: Defect in the diaphragm (left-sided ~85%) allowing abdominal organs to herniate into the chest → pulmonary hypoplasia + pulmonary hypertension. Incidence: ~1/2,500 births.

  • Diagnosis: Often prenatal (US). Postnatal: scaphoid abdomen, barrel chest, absent breath sounds on affected side, bowel sounds in chest, displaced heart sounds, respiratory distress
  • CXR: Bowel loops in thorax, mediastinal shift away from hernia, nasogastric tube in chest
  • Severity depends on degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and PPHN

Delivery Room Management:

  1. IMMEDIATE intubation — do NOT bag-mask ventilate (inflates stomach/bowel in chest, compresses lungs further)
  2. Large-bore OG tube to continuous suction — decompress stomach and bowel
  3. Gentle ventilation: low PIP (<25 cmH₂O), avoid high PEEP (>5 cmH₂O)
  4. Pre-ductal SpO₂ monitoring (right hand) — accept SpO₂ 80–95% initially
  5. Umbilical lines — UVC and UAC for access and monitoring
  6. NO chest compressions on affected side
  7. Avoid high-frequency ventilation initially (can overdistend contralateral lung)
🚨 Do NOT bag-mask ventilate CDH. This inflates bowel in the chest and worsens lung compression. Intubate immediately.

Gentle Ventilation Strategy (CDH EURO Consortium):

  • PIP <25 cmH₂O (permissive hypercapnia: accept PaCO₂ up to 65 mmHg if pH >7.20)
  • PEEP 3–5 cmH₂O
  • Pre-ductal SpO₂ target: 80–95% initially, >85% after stabilization
  • iNO for PPHN component (variable response — pulmonary hypoplasia limits iNO effectiveness)
  • ECMO if failing maximal medical therapy (survival ~50% for CDH-ECMO, lower than non-CDH respiratory ECMO)
  • Surgical repair: Delayed until physiologic stabilization (typically 24–72h or when PPHN controlled). Emergent surgery is NOT indicated.
